problem.title: Most site data dies in a folder.
problem.lead: A survey flight produces gigabytes of truth about a site. Then it gets exported, zipped, emailed once, and never opened again. Three reasons:

reasons.title: The file needs a specialist.
reasons.body: Point clouds and meshes open in software the client, the site manager and the investor do not have and will not install.

reasons.title: It is a snapshot, not a record.
reasons.body: One flight, one moment. Nothing links this month's reality to last month's.

reasons.title: The knowledge stays with one person.
reasons.body: Measurements, volumes and notes live in someone's project folder.

problem.quote: A model nobody can open is not documentation. It is storage.

engine.title: One engine: capture, model, twin.
engine.lead: The same three steps run over every site. Only the subject changes.

steps.name: Capture
steps.body: RTK drone flights for exteriors and terrain. 360° camera for interiors and walkthroughs. Planned overlap and ground control, so it is measurable.

steps.name: Model
steps.body: Photogrammetric processing to point cloud and textured mesh. Digital terrain models, contours, areas and volumes. Exports engineers already use: Revit, Civil 3D, AutoCAD, .dwg.

steps.name: Twin
steps.body: Opens in a browser: no download, no plugin, no licence. Information layers on top of geometry: keypoints, notes, measurements. Re-fly it and the twin gains a timeline instead of a replacement.

formats.title: It has to open in what you already have.
formats.lead: A deliverable is worth nothing if opening it needs a licence you do not own. Every export lands in a format your engineers already work in, and the twin needs no software at all.

droneMapping.h1: Drone mapping that holds up when someone measures it.
droneMapping.lead: The flight is the easy part. What decides whether the survey was worth paying for is whether the output survives a second opinion, so we plan overlap, use RTK positioning, and put ground control on the site when the accuracy target needs it.

faq.intro: Direct answers, no sales gloss. Anything missing, ask us.

items.q: What is a digital twin, and how is it different from a 3D model?
items.a: A 3D model shows shape and texture. A digital twin adds an information layer on top, keypoints, notes and measurements, it opens in any browser, and every capture is kept, so change over time stays visible. In short: the model shows the place, the twin explains it.

items.q: What deliverables does a drone capture produce?
items.a: Point cloud, textured mesh, digital terrain models, contours, measured areas and volumes, and exports in formats engineers already use: Revit, Civil 3D, AutoCAD, .dwg.

items.q: Do I need special software to open the results?
items.a: No. The twin opens in any web browser on any device, with no download, plugin or licence. CAD deliverables such as .dwg open in the tools your engineers already have.

items.q: Are the models measurable, or just visual?
items.a: Measurable. Flights use RTK positioning, planned overlap, and ground control points where accuracy demands it.

Our own construction progress-tracking platform. You give your client a login; they see stage-by-stage progress, media updates, milestones and materials, and each drone capture as a phase with 3D models and 360° tours, all in the browser.

items.q: Which sectors do you work in?
items.a: Construction and residential, quarries and extraction, heritage and archaeology, real estate, wind and energy assets, agriculture and land, and large indoor spaces. The pipeline is the same everywhere; only the deliverable changes.

With one phone call. You describe the site and what you need to measure or prove, and we tell you plainly what can be captured and what cannot. Then one visit for the flight, processing, and delivery.
We are based in Athens and work all over Greece. We also take on projects abroad, in the EU and beyond: tell us where your site is.

items.q: The site keeps changing. Do we capture again?
items.a: Yes, that is the point. Each new flight is added as a phase, the twin gains a timeline, and the change between captures becomes visible.
